en: We shall now explain the measure of each foot, their number, and their divisions, as well as the twelve-spoked wheel which is further divided into two parts. (1)
One should divide each half-mora into fifteen parts;
[this is for] Śiva in the form of Oṃkāra, and for Śivā who possesses the form of Oṃkāra. (2)
At the base of the eastern spoke, to the south of Vyopikāra, there is no such placement of the mantra step by step in this clockwise manner. (3)
One who desires accomplishment should perform the ritual up to the "all-ending" (sarvāntika) stage;
thereafter, one should place the bone-syllable (sthī), the bone-syllable again, and that very same syllable with the visarga.
The protracted vowels, the particles, the letter *piṃ*, the letter *ā* in the same way, the letter *a* in *namāyātama*, the letters *va*, *ca*, *ve*, and then *añca*. || 5 ||
The letter *bha* is not so [in its nature] as the three syllables *tī*, *kṣi*, and *jñā*;
the letter *ma* is manifold, while *tā* and *tāś* are for the purpose of destruction; therefore, it is the imperishable (*akṣara*).

The letters *dha*, *na*, *ya*, *pra*, *śca*, *ru*, *tā*, *ca*, *ni*, *pa*, *śca*, *pra*, *u*, *ta*, *taḥ*, *dhya*, *śca*, *cci*, *śca*, *ta*, *tu*, *śca*, *ta*, *sau*, and *ca* occur in the two quarters [of the verse]. (7)
Then *vyā*, *śi*, *yā*, *ya*, *ca*, *vā*, *yu*, *ca*, *vā*, *ta*, *tā*, *pā*, likewise *s* and *tha*, the letter *pa*, the vowels other than the lower ones (*adharāḥ*), and then *ra* and *ma*. (8)

One who has ceased with the letter *bha*, and one who knows the tree (*tarujña*); then one who dwells at the end (*vāstataḥ*), and one who drinks the waters (*pibādhrūni*), and one whose self is restrained (*yatatmā*), and one who liberates (*mocayaḥ*), and one who moves (*cara*). 9.
Then there were Mīñca and Aśva, the first of the names, as well as Ātha, Varāva, and likewise Neiyava. || 10 ||
The seven-syllable [pāda] is repeated twice; at the end, however, there are two six-syllable pādas, and then another four-syllable [pāda]. || 11 ||
Then there are five syllables of three letters each, and two others in a group of four letters; after that, one should know the word "śivottama," and then the two words "om" and "bhūḥ."
Then there is Ekanetra, followed by another [mantra] consisting of one syllable and one of two syllables,
within an arrangement of words beginning with the syllable Oṃ and comprising thirty-four words.
He is to be known as Ekarudra; from him comes Trimūrti, who has three feet.
Śrīkaṇṭha then possesses six feet, and another foot belongs to Śikhaṇḍin.
Thus is the division of mantras established within the essence of Śiva’s body.
Now, it should be known that from the fifty [phonemes], there is one syllable and two words. 15.
The four-syllable [name], the three-syllable, and again another two-syllable word;
furthermore, the five-syllable word, and then two two-syllable words. (16)
From this [word], there are three syllables of four letters each; from that, the five-syllabled word arises.
There are four, five, four, six, and four syllables respectively.
There are five words here; the fourth is the weapon-mantra (astra) of the limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅga).
Then there is a word of four syllables, another of four syllables, and thereafter a word of eight syllables. || 18 ||
Seven, eight, and six syllables are to be known as those three feet;
then from them, there are three feet consisting of five syllables and four syllables respectively. 19.
Thereafter, from the six-syllable [mantra], there are four groups of four syllables;
then again two syllables each, and then a word of three syllables.

That which consists of one syllable, two syllables, or three syllables is to be known as a single-syllabled [word]; furthermore, it should be understood that a word may consist of two syllables or two feet, while a foot, moreover, consists of three syllables. || 21 ||
There are two other words consisting of two syllables each; such is the proclaimed number of words.
The syllable *oṃ* at the end of all [the words] is proclaimed to belong to Śiva.
Having understood the collection of phonemes in this [system], as well as the arising of mantras and the arising of the stages,
one who worships the Self that is the year, having performed the sacrifice, goes to the auspicious state.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, concerning the characteristics of Śiva-mantras, in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṅgraha.
